description:
I am Amine Kacem, a Geomatics Engineering student specializing in remote sensing, spatial data pipelines, and GeoAI. My focus is on leveraging Earth Observation datasets to build scalable environmental monitoring tools and cloud-native spatial applications.

Happy to participate in this event.
summary: On the night of 17 June 2026, a 72-year-old gate failed at the Mellègue dam in Nebeur, northwest Tunisia. The press reported about 21 million m³ of water released toward the Sidi Salem reservoir. Dancing with the Rivers replays that night, and the month after it, in 3D from real radar data. Our web app, Dancing with the Rivers, measures the lake on NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band and Sentinel-1 images and explains each radar signal in plain language. It checks the radar against SWOT lake heights: the water surface fell 3.75 m between 7 and 28 June. NISAR and Sentinel-1 together would have raised an alarm on 22 June, five days after the failure, with no ground sensor. The story then opens Dam Watch: lake area, automatic alerts, level change and labelled "what if" flood scenarios down to Sidi Salem. Tunisia's daily dam bulletins stopped in October 2025, so free, independent monitoring matters.
details:
What it does

Dancing with the Rivers uses open satellite data to reconstruct one real event, the gate failure at the Mellègue dam on 17 June, and then hands the reader a working tool, Dam Watch, that monitors a reservoir from space. The story is told in nine short acts.

Every layer and number carries a badge, MEASURED, REPORTED, MODELLED or ILLUSTRATIVE, with its source. Uncertainty is drawn as bands and ranges, so the reader always sees what was observed and what was computed.

How it works

An offline Python pipeline turns satellite data into a small, versioned data bundle, and the web app reads only that bundle: no server, no keys, no live API calls. The pipeline has six stages.

1. Water area (MEASURED). NISAR GCOV backscatter (HH, L-band) and Sentinel-1 RTC (VV, C-band) are thresholded image by image with Otsu's method, applied inside the lake and a 300 m ring around it. The water area is then counted inside the pre-failure lake polygon (4.69 km², built from 19 pre-failure Sentinel-1 images). A fixed −18 dB threshold was tested and failed: wind roughens the lake at C-band, and wet mud looks like water at L-band.

2. Alerts (MODELLED). Each new area is compared with the median of the previous 21 days. WARNING is raised below −12% and ALERT below −20%, each confirmed by an independent pass within 6 days. The first ALERT came on 22 June (Sentinel-1 orbit 161, −20.5%, confirmed by orbit 88, −28.8%). The rule raised no flag in the 14 evaluations before the failure, and the first NISAR flag came on 26 June (track A173, WARNING, −13%).

3. Level and volume (MEASURED / MODELLED). SWOT LakeSP heights are pulled through Hydrocron (lake 1530007983, 19 passes kept). The level fell from 260.54 m on 7 June to 256.79 m on 28 June, a change of −3.75 ± 0.08 m. Storage change is the area multiplied by the level change between the two passes: −12.7 million m³ (range 7.8 to 17.1).

4. Flow path and quick flood (MODELLED). D8 routing on Google's GEM-15 terrain (15 m, averaged to 30 m) gives the 101 km path, and 98.8% of it lies within 300 m of mapped rivers. A HAND "bathtub" lookup converts any volume into a water height and an exposed area, directly in the browser.

5. Physics scenarios (MODELLED). The ANUGA 2D shallow-water model runs from the dam to the Medjerda confluence (112 km², 69,616 triangles) with a 12-hour triangular release of 21, 50 or 195 million m³. For 21 million m³ the front reaches the confluence after about 13 h (19 h on a coarser mesh, so timing is mesh-sensitive).

6. Exposure (MODELLED). Wet cells are crossed with ESA WorldCover (cropland, built-up), OpenStreetMap (roads, buildings, villages) and WorldPop.

The web application

The front end is built with React and TypeScript. It has a three.js 3D scene of the real valley, a cinematic intro, and story cards at two levels (Everyone and Experts). Data contracts are written once with pydantic and checked on both sides, with JSON Schema in Python and Zod in the browser, so the pipeline and the app cannot drift apart.

Tools, languages and hardware

What comes next

The next step is a measured one: run the same steps on 5 to 10 more reservoirs in northern Tunisia as an offline batch, and only then build a live service.

1. Scale out (offline batch). Apply the pipeline to Sidi Salem, Bou Heurtma, Beni Mtir, Kasseb and other reservoirs.

2. Validate. Measure the alert rule's detection and false-alarm rates on dams it was not tuned on. Today the thresholds (−12% and −20%, 21-day median, 6-day confirmation) are tuned on Mellègue alone.

3. Go live. Only after validation, build a live service on top of the proven rule.
